docs.title: UiPath Cartographer Tech Workshop
docs.text:
Design a real business process with UiPath Cartographer, from raw discovery evidence to a reviewed PDD, and see how that design carries on all the way to production.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant CartographerWorkshop.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
Cartographer is UiPath's agentic process-design tool. You give it a brief and the evidence a team already has, and it maps the current state, designs the future state, and writes the documentation. It asks only about real gaps, recommends an answer, and leaves the decision to you. Every fact it captures is traced back to its source.

The workshop has two exercises. The first one is fully hands-on. The second one picks up where the first leaves off.

Warranty Resolution at Cobalt Ridge Automation: Cobalt Ridge Automation handles about 7,400 warranty claims a year. A claim takes 11.4 days to resolve, and a P1 line outage keeps a customer's production down for 96 hours. Your brief: get resolution down to 3.5 days and P1 downtime down to 24 hours. You'll take the process from a blank project to a published Process Definition Document (PDD) and an SDD generated from it. Along the way you'll build a current-state wiki with provenance on every fact, choose how to map today's process, design a future state where every change is argued against a KPI, make live edits that stay inside compliance guardrails, and publish the PDD and SDD to Automation Hub.

From Process to Production: The Documentation isn't the end of the story. This exercise follows the design downstream: in VS Code, a coding agent such as Claude Code builds one of your Maestro Flow stages from the Solution Design Document (SDD) with the UiPath skills, and you deploy it to Orchestrator and open it in Studio Web. Runtime insights then flow back into the Map of Work, so the design keeps improving.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• UiPath Cartographer: discovers how work really happens, then makes it ready to build. A guided, AI-powered discovery conversation turns scattered process knowledge into one living definition of how the work runs. It starts with context, asks only what's missing, reconciles your evidence and routes questions to the experts who know.
  • Map of Work: the source of truth: one living, customer-owned definition of how the work actually runs, stored in your tenant. It holds the people, stages, systems and data, rules, exceptions, judgment and goals. Every Map of Work is versioned, has a named owner and approver, carries provenance on every fact, and uses an open, portable format, the Open Knowledge Format (OKF).
  • Process Atlas: UiPath's library of curated, expert-attested Maps of Work for verticalized processes, organized by industry, process area and process. It covers industries such as banking, insurance, healthcare, manufacturing, telecom and utilities. You adapt a proven map instead of drawing from a blank page, and every map improves with expert reviews and live deployments.
  • Provenance: every fact in the Map of Work is attributable. Each element carries its source and its verifier, and contradictions between sources are resolved, not averaged.
  • AS-IS and TO-BE: the process as it really runs today, grounded in your evidence and your experts, and the agreed future process you design against your KPIs and objectives.
  • Process Definition Document (PDD): generated from the Map of Work for decision-makers. It describes what the process does, why, and the value it delivers.
  • Solution Design Document (SDD): generated from the Map of Work for developers and coding agents. It describes how to build the solution on the UiPath Platform.
  • Best-fit canvas: Cartographer's recommendation of the Maestro canvas that suits the work best: Case, BPMN or Flow, with the reasoning behind it.
  • Automation Hub: the UiPath process repository, where the PDD, the process map and the solution live together.

Next: Warranty Resolution at Cobalt Ridge

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
You've reached the end of the workshop

You've taken a real process from scattered evidence to a published PDD, and followed that design all the way to production.

docs.title: Keep building
docs.text:
• Map a process of your own. Bring the SOPs, recordings and workshop notes you already have, and let Cartographer ask only what's missing.
  • Start from Process Atlas. For banking, insurance, healthcare, manufacturing, telecom and utilities processes, adapt an expert-attested Map of Work instead of starting from a blank page.
  • Change the map and regenerate. Edit a business rule or a stage in your Map of Work, then regenerate the PDD and SDD and see what changes downstream.

docs.title: From Process to Production
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this exercise:

  1. See how the PDD and SDD you just published travel on, from design to build, run and improvement.
  2. Review the Solution Design Document (SDD) you generated in Cartographer and sign it off.
  3. Set up VS Code with the UiPath Maestro extension and a coding agent.
  4. Have the coding agent build one of your Maestro Flow stages from the SDD, then validate it, deploy it to Orchestrator and open it in Studio Web.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
By the end of this exercise you'll have followed one design all the way down the line. One stage of the Cobalt Ridge SDD you generated in the first exercise becomes a working Maestro Flow, deployed to Orchestrator and open in Studio Web for your team. You'll also see how a change to the map finds its way back to the people, and the agents, who maintain the automation.

Next: The Documentation isn't the end of the story

docs.title: Optional: build the whole case
docs.text: You built one stage. If you're ahead of the clock, or you want to try the full path after the workshop, a coding agent can build the whole Cobalt Ridge case from the same SDD. This page gives you the pointers. It isn't a step-by-step exercise.

docs.title: The skills involved
docs.text:
The uip skills install command you ran earlier already installed these UiPath skills. Your coding agent loads them on its own when the task calls for them:

Skill What it does uipath-planner Reads the SDD and turns it into a design and a list of build tasks across UiPath products. uipath-maestro-case Builds the Maestro case plan (caseplan.case) and resolves the tenant resources it needs. uipath-maestro-flow Builds the Flow stages, the same skill you used in this exercise. uipath-solution Packs, publishes and deploys the solution.

docs.title: How to start
docs.text:
1. Create a new empty folder, open it in VS Code and copy the SDD into it.

  2. Ask your coding agent, for example:

    Create a uipath maestro case project using the SDD file in this folder. Prefix the name of every artifact you create with {YourName}.

  3. Let it plan first. Read the task list it derives from the SDD before it starts building, and answer its questions.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Give it time. A whole case has many stages, agents, human tasks and connections. Expect a long run with many tool calls.
  • Reuse your Flow. Tell the agent about the Flow you already built, so it links that stage instead of building it again.
  • Review in Studio Web. The VS Code extension shows Flow on a canvas. Review the case plan in Studio Web after you upload or deploy the solution.
  • Expect gaps. As with your Flow, connections that don't exist in the tenant become placeholders or questions. Check the agent's list of what's missing.
  • Watch your usage. A full build consumes far more of your AI usage allowance than a single Flow.

Next: Next steps

docs.title: Build your Flow with a coding agent
docs.text: In the first exercise, you asked Cartographer to run two stages of the Cobalt Ridge case with Maestro Flow. Now you'll pick one of them and have your coding agent build it, straight from the SDD.

docs.title: 1. Create the Maestro project
docs.text:
1. Create an empty parent folder for your work, for example {YourName}-Cobalt, and open it in VS Code (File > Open Folder).
  2. When VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files in this folder, click Yes, I trust the authors. In Restricted Mode, extensions are turned off and the UiPath icon doesn't load. If you closed the prompt, run Workspaces: Manage Workspace Trust from the Command Palette and trust the folder.
  3. Click the UiPath icon in the Activity Bar. In the UiPath Maestro view, click Create New and choose Maestro Orchestrate from the New Project list.
  4. Name the solution and the project with your name as a prefix, for example {YourName}_CobaltFlow. The extension scaffolds the solution in its own subfolder, with the project and a default .flow file, and opens it in a new VS Code window.
  5. Switch to that new window and keep working there. Its folder is the solution folder: it holds the .uipx solution file, and packaging and deploying only work from it. Trust this folder too if VS Code asks.

Why the name prefix?

Everyone in the workshop builds in the same tenant. A {YourName} prefix keeps your solutions, processes and connections from colliding with your neighbour's.

docs.title: 2. Add the SDD to the folder
docs.text: Copy the SDD you downloaded in Review the SDD into the solution folder, the one open in the new window, or unzip the example SDD there. Your coding agent reads it from there.

docs.title: 3. Pick your stage
docs.text:
Choose one of the two stages you assigned to Maestro Flow in the first exercise:

  • Asset, Entitlement and Evidence Readiness (Warranty Asset and Evidence Readiness Flow in the SDD): resolves the asset, verifies the entitlement, retrieves the evidence and scores readiness before coverage is decided.
  • Cost reconciliation (Warranty Cost Reconciliation Flow in the SDD): assembles the actual costs, posts and reconciles them, calculates the variance and routes anything above 20% to Finance for verification.

docs.title: 4. Ask your coding agent to build it
docs.text:
Send the prompt for your stage to your coding agent, then replace {YourName} with your name:

Asset, Entitlement and Evidence ReadinessCost reconciliation 
Read the SDD file in this folder for the Cobalt Ridge warranty resolution process. Build only the Maestro Flow for the "Asset, Entitlement and Evidence Readiness" stage, in this project's .flow file, following that stage's section of the SDD. If an Integration Service connection or another resource the flow needs doesn't exist in my tenant, use a placeholder node and list what's missing at the end. Prefix the name of every artifact you create with {YourName}.

Read the SDD file in this folder for the Cobalt Ridge warranty resolution process. Build only the Maestro Flow for the cost reconciliation stage, in this project's .flow file, following that stage's section of the SDD. If an Integration Service connection or another resource the flow needs doesn't exist in my tenant, use a placeholder node and list what's missing at the end. Prefix the name of every artifact you create with {YourName}.

The agent loads the UiPath skills for Maestro Flow, reads the SDD and looks up the nodes, connectors and resources available in your tenant. Then it builds the flow.

  1. Keep the .flow file open. You can watch the nodes appear on the canvas as the agent adds them.
  2. Answer the agent's questions as they come up, and approve commands as it runs them.
  3. When it's done, read its summary, especially the list of placeholders and anything missing from the tenant.

Placeholders are expected

The SDD names systems such as SAP S/4HANA and FieldLink. The workshop tenant doesn't have connections to all of them, so some steps stay as placeholders. That's fine: the structure of the stage, its decisions and its handoffs are what you're building today.

docs.title: 5. Make it yours
docs.text:
The canvas works like the one in Studio Web. Select a node to check its configuration and variables, and adjust anything the agent got wrong, either by hand or by asking the agent. For example, ask it to rename a node or to add a missing decision from the SDD.

Next: Validate, deploy and open it in Studio Web

docs.title: Close the loop
docs.text:
1. In Automation Hub, open the process map and choose Edit Process Model.
  2. Make a small change to the model and save it.

When an analyst changes the model, the developers or coding agents who own the automation are notified to update it. Runtime insights from the running process flow back into the Map of Work. That's the Improve stage: the design and the automation keep improving together, long after the PDD was signed off.

Next: Optional: build the whole case

docs.title: Review the SDD
docs.text:
Before you begin: prerequisites

Have these ready before you start:

  • The first exercise, finished: your Cobalt Ridge project, with the PDD and the SDD published to Automation Hub.
  • VS Code 1.110.0 or later and Node.js: you'll install the UiPath Maestro extension on the next page.
  • A coding agent: this guide uses Claude Code.
  • Access to the workshop environment: in this workshop we use https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs/CartographerWorkshop. Talk to your trainer if you haven't received an invitation.

docs.title: 1. Open the SDD you generated
docs.text:
Go back to your Cobalt Ridge project in Cartographer. At the end of the first exercise, Cartographer turned your TO-BE into a Solution Design Document (SDD): a solution architecture on the UiPath Platform, built around Maestro case orchestration, with the Maestro Flow stages you chose and the AI agents, human-in-the-loop tasks and integrations your design calls for. Now it's time to check it before anything gets built.

  1. Open Solution design (SDD) in the left navigation. Walk the table of contents: process overview, diagram, activities, gateways and events, data objects, integrated components, error handling, triggers, project structure, testing strategy and next steps.
  2. Read the summary in the conversation. It lists the status, the template validation result, the architecture, what the SDD covers, the result of an independent review, and any open items. Open items are tagged [SME REVIEW] so you know exactly what still needs a human answer.

docs.title: 2. Mark it as reviewed and download it
docs.text:
1. Cartographer deliberately leaves the build hand-off open until you approve the design. Mark the SDD as reviewed in the document panel.
  2. Click Download to save the SDD. You'll hand this file to the coding agent.

No SDD, or yours is incomplete?

Download the example SDD from the Cobalt Ridge run and start from it. It's a Markdown file, ready for your coding agent, with both Maestro Flow stages included.

Download the example SDD (.zip)

Why this matters

The build never starts from an unreviewed design. A person signs off on the SDD before any coding agent touches it.

Next: Set up VS Code and the Maestro extension

docs.title: Set up VS Code and the Maestro extension
docs.text: You'll build your Flow in Visual Studio Code with the UiPath Maestro extension and a coding agent. This page gets all three ready and signed in to the workshop tenant.

docs.title: 1. Install VS Code and Node.js
docs.text:
1. Install VS Code version 1.110.0 or later from code.visualstudio.com. If it's already installed, check your version under Help > About and update if needed.
  2. Install Node.js (the LTS version) from nodejs.org. npm comes with it, and the extension uses npm to install the uip CLI. Keep the installer's Add to PATH option selected.
  3. Close VS Code completely and open it again. Its terminal doesn't see newly installed programs until VS Code restarts.

  4. Open a terminal in VS Code (Terminal > New Terminal) and check both versions:

    node --version
npm --version

    Each command prints a version number. If you get "not recognized" or "command not found", run the Node.js installer again with Add to PATH selected, then restart VS Code.

Remote workspaces

If you work in WSL, over SSH, in Codespaces or in a dev container, install Node.js and npm on the remote host, not on your local machine.

docs.title: 2. Install the UiPath Maestro extension
docs.text:
The extension is published by UiPath on the Visual Studio Marketplace. You can install it from inside VS Code:

  1. In VS Code, open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X, or Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac).
  2. Search for UiPath Maestro.
  3. Check that the publisher is UiPath and the extension ID is uipath.uipath-maestro, then click Install.
  4. Reload VS Code if it asks you to.

You can also open the extension page on the Marketplace and click Install there. When the install finishes, a UiPath icon appears in the Activity Bar on the left.

docs.title: 3. Sign in to the workshop tenant
docs.text:
1. Click the UiPath icon in the Activity Bar.
  2. In the Connect section, click Sign In.
  3. If the extension offers to install the CLI, accept. It runs npm install -g @uipath/cli for you.
  4. Finish the sign-in in the browser window that opens. The sign-in returns to VS Code through localhost port 8104, so keep that port free.
  5. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac) and run UiPath: Select Environment. Keep Cloud.
  6. Run UiPath: Select Tenant and pick CartographerWorkshop.

docs.title: Check that the CLI is installed
docs.text:
The extension's Get started page shows a checklist at the top: Signed in, CLI installed with its version, and AI skills. You can also check in the terminal:

uip --version

If it prints a version, you're set. If you get "not recognized" or "command not found", the extension didn't install it. Install it yourself, then restart VS Code:

npm install -g @uipath/cli

docs.title: 4. Get your coding agent ready
docs.text:
The coding agent needs the uip CLI signed in to the same tenant as the extension, plus the UiPath skills that teach it how to build on UiPath.

  1. In the VS Code terminal (Terminal > New Terminal), check the CLI session:

    uip login status

    If it isn't signed in to CartographerWorkshop, sign in:

    uip login --authority https://cloud.uipath.com -t CartographerWorkshop

  2. Check the CLI tools. The CLI works through tools, one per product area. List them:

    uip tools list --output table

    For this exercise you need maestro-tool and solution-tool, plus orchestrator-tool and integrationservice-tool for the deploy and the connections. Install any that are missing, one at a time:

    uip tools install maestro
uip tools install solution
uip tools install orchestrator
uip tools install integrationservice

    If any of them shows needs update, run uip tools update.

  3. Install the UiPath skills for your coding agent. This example is for Claude Code; for another agent, change the --agent value (for example cursor, copilot or codex):

    uip skills install --agent claude

  4. Open your coding agent. This guide uses Claude Code, either through its VS Code extension or by running claude in the VS Code terminal.

Sessions, identity, and security

The agent uses your session and acts with your permissions. Approve its uip commands one by one as they come up, rather than allowing all of them at once.

Next: Build your Flow with a coding agent

docs.title: The Documentation isn't the end of the story
docs.text:
In most organizations, a process document is where the work stops being visible. It gets attached to an email, someone rebuilds it as a slide, and the developer who finally builds the automation never sees the evidence behind it.

On the UiPath Platform, the design keeps moving. Here's the journey:

DiscoverCartographer DocumentPDD and SDD BuildCoding agents with UiPath skills CollaborateAutomation Hub and Studio Web RunOrchestrator and Maestro ImproveRuntime insights feed the Map of Work

Filled dots: the stages where Cartographer works. Open dots: where the rest of the UiPath Platform takes over.

Stage What happens Discover Cartographer captures the process from your evidence. It asks only about real gaps, recommends an answer, and you decide. Document The PDD says what the process does and why. The SDD says how to build it. Every document is generated from the Map of Work, never invented, and changing a fact updates only the sections built from it. Build A coding agent such as Claude Code reads the SDD. The UiPath skills teach it how to build on UiPath, so it can plan the tasks, build the solution and test it. Collaborate The documentation goes to the Process Repository in Automation Hub, next to the process map. The solution goes to Studio Web, where your team can review and own it. Run The solution is deployed to Orchestrator and runs as an agentic process in Maestro: agents, robots and people working on the same case. Improve Analysts refine the process map themselves. Developers and coding agents are notified to update the automation, and runtime insights flow back into the Map of Work.

The same design is carried from the first interview to the running process. Nobody retypes it, and it keeps its link to the evidence and to the KPI it serves.

Next: Review the SDD

docs.title: Validate, deploy and open it in Studio Web
docs.text: Your Flow is on the canvas. Now you'll check it, run it, put it in Orchestrator and open it in Studio Web, where your team can review and own it.

docs.title: 1. Validate the Flow
docs.text:
1. With the .flow file open, run Flow: Validate Flow from the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+V, or Cmd+Shift+V on a Mac).
  2. Open the Problems panel (View > Problems). Problems also appear there while you edit.

  3. If anything is listed, ask your coding agent to fix it, for example:

    Fix the validation problems in the .flow file.

Go on once validation shows no errors.

docs.title: 2. Run it and watch it work
docs.text:
1. Run the flow from the editor.
  2. Follow the live debug view. It draws the execution as a flowchart and updates it as each node runs, so you can see which path your stage took and where a placeholder stopped it.

docs.title: 3. Package and deploy to Orchestrator
docs.text:
1. Run UiPath: Switch Deploy Target and choose the workshop folder your trainer gives you.
  2. Run UiPath: Package & Deploy. The extension builds a .uipx solution package and uploads it to Orchestrator.

The deployment is activated automatically, so your process is ready to run as soon as the command finishes.

\"No UiPath solution found in this workspace\"?

VS Code has the parent folder open instead of the solution folder. Use File > Open Folder to open the folder that contains the .uipx file, then run UiPath: Package & Deploy again.

If there's no .uipx file anywhere, the Flow was built outside a solution. Create one next to your project folder, move the project folder into it, and register it:

uip solution init {YourName}_CobaltFlow
uip solution projects add "<path to your project folder>"

Then open the new solution folder in VS Code and package again.

Two steps instead of one

UiPath: Package and UiPath: Deploy run the same two steps separately, if you want to check the package before you upload it.

docs.title: 4. Find it in Orchestrator
docs.text:
1. Sign in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs and open Orchestrator in the CartographerWorkshop tenant.
  2. Open the folder you deployed to. Your {YourName} process is listed under Automations > Processes.

docs.title: 5. Open it in Studio Web
docs.text:
To edit and review the Flow in the browser, upload the solution to Studio Web:

  1. In the VS Code terminal, go to your solution folder, the one that holds the .uipx solution, not the project folder inside it.

  2. Upload it:

    uip solution upload "<path to your solution folder>"

    If you upload the same solution again later, add --force to replace the earlier upload.

  3. Open Studio Web from https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs and find your {YourName} solution.

  4. Open the Flow project. It's the same flow you built in VS Code, on the same canvas, ready for your team.

Why this matters

The SDD from Cartographer became a working Flow in Orchestrator, and the same Flow is open for review in Studio Web. Nobody retyped the design along the way.

Next: Close the loop

docs.title: Warranty Resolution at Cobalt Ridge Automation
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this exercise:

  1. Create a Cartographer project, give it the business brief, and check what it already knows.
  2. Feed it the evidence a real team would have and review the current state (AS-IS) it builds.
  3. Design the future state (TO-BE), make a live edit, and verify it landed everywhere.
  4. Generate the PDD and trace your edits inside it.
  5. Generate the SDD, bring in Maestro Flow for the stages that suit it, and publish both documents to Automation Hub.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
By the end of this exercise you'll have taken one process from a blank project to a published Process Definition Document (PDD). You'll have a current-state wiki with provenance on every fact, a future-state design where every change is tied to a specific KPI, and a PDD that carries your own edits. From that PDD you'll generate a Solution Design Document (SDD) and publish both to Automation Hub.

Next: How Cartographer works

docs.title: About Cobalt Ridge Automation
docs.text: Cobalt Ridge Automation builds industrial automation and material-handling equipment, in other words: the machines that keep goods moving inside warehouses and factories (conveyor belts, sorters and the controls that run them). You probably never notice this kind of equipment, until it stops. When a customer's sortation line goes down, getting it running again involves people across the company, and no single process ties their work together.

docs.title: What's a sortation line?
docs.text:
Picture a big parcel hub on a busy morning. Thousands of packages arrive on conveyor belts. Scanners read every barcode, and the system pushes each package down the right chute, toward the right truck or the right order. That automated sorting system is a sortation line, and Cobalt Ridge sells them to its customers.

When a sortation line goes down, the warehouse can't ship. Packages pile up, trucks leave half empty and orders go out late. Cobalt Ridge calls this a P1 line outage, the most urgent kind of problem there is. Every hour it lasts costs the customer money and patience.

docs.title: What's a warranty claim?
docs.text:
When a customer buys a line, Cobalt Ridge promises to fix it for free if something breaks during an agreed period. That promise is the warranty. A warranty claim is the customer calling to say: "It broke, it's still covered, please fix it."

Cobalt Ridge made the equipment and made the promise, so the claim lands on its desk. Every claim costs it parts, technician time and sometimes credits to an unhappy customer. And there are a lot of them:

~7,400warranty claims a year 11.4 daysmean time from customer report to restored line 96 hoursmean downtime for a P1 line outage $23.8Mannual warranty spend

docs.title: Seven teams, one relay race
docs.text:
Getting a broken line running again isn't one person's job. Seven functions pass the claim along like a baton:

SupportWarranty administrationEngineeringPartsField serviceFinanceQuality
  1. Support takes the customer's call and logs the problem.
  2. Warranty administration checks whether the equipment is still covered. Today that decision waits for a weekly review, so a claim can wait up to a week for an answer.
  3. Engineering works out what's actually wrong.
  4. Parts finds and ships the replacement. Sometimes it swaps in a substitute part and nobody writes it down.
  5. Field service sends a technician to fix the line on site.
  6. Finance records what the repair cost, often late.
  7. Quality should spot the parts that keep failing. Often it never hears about them.

The baton doesn't travel well. The work is spread across six systems and one very long email thread:

Support Cloud (CRSC)WarrantyTrack WT-9AssetVaultHelios CRMSAP S/4HANAFieldLink FSMEmail

People retype the same details from one system into the next, handoffs get lost in inboxes, and repeat failures go unnoticed because nobody connects the dots. Add it all up and you get 11.4 days per claim and $23.8M a year.

docs.title: Your mission
docs.text:
Cobalt Ridge's leadership has set a clear target for FY2027. You'll use Cartographer to redesign the process so it gets there.

The brief for FY2027

11.4 days→3.5 daysmean resolution time 96 hours→24 hoursP1 line downtime

People keep authority over coverage, safety, engineering, substitution, restoration and finance decisions. Your job is to design how.

Next: Get your machine ready

docs.title: Optional: ask a teammate
docs.text:
Only run this if you're ahead of the clock. Pair up, so someone is there to answer.

Is 20% the right variance threshold? Instead of guessing, delegate the question to finance from inside the conversation.

  1. Use Ask a teammate to write your question.

  2. Generate the shareable link and send it to your partner.

The link opens a session for your colleague with the question and its context already loaded. Their answer lands back in your conversation, ready for you to accept.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs and remember using tenant CartographerWorkshop for this exercise.

Next: From Process to Production

docs.title: 1. Add the evidence
docs.text:
The evidence pack is the kind of material a team already has: process flows from two departments, a process-owner interview, a workshop transcript, an executive brief, a systems architecture draft and a printed claim record.

  1. Download the evidence pack and unzip it anywhere on the machine you're working on, the workshop VM or your own:

    Download the Cobalt Ridge evidence pack (.zip)

    Using the workshop VM?

    Open this workshop site in a browser on the VM, at https://uipath-practice.github.io/CartographerWorkshop/, and download the pack from there. That way the files land on the VM, where you'll attach them.

  2. Attach the files listed below and send them with this prompt:

    Add to the AS-IS references.

Files to attach:

  • a_process_flows/CobaltRidge_FieldService-and-Parts_Dispatch-and-Fulfillment_AS-IS.svg
  • a_process_flows/CobaltRidge_Support-and-Warranty-Admin_Claim-Intake-and-Adjudication_CURRENT-STATE.pptx
  • b_process_owner_interview/Interview_Priya-Raghunathan_Warranty-Process-Owner_2026-02-19.docx
  • c_workshop_transcript/Workshop-Transcript_Warranty-Resolution-Current-State_2026-03-26.docx
  • d_executive_brief/CobaltRidge_Warranty-Resolution-Transformation_Executive-Brief_FY2027.pptx
  • e_systems_architecture/CobaltRidge_Warranty-Systems-Architecture_Current-State_v0.9-DRAFT.docx
  • e_systems_architecture/CobaltRidge_Warranty-Systems-Landscape_Current-State.svg
  • f_claim_record/WC-2026-04871_WarrantyTrack-WT9_Full-Claim-Record_PRINTED.docx

Leave these two files out

  • 00_START_HERE_BA-notes.md: background for the facilitator, not input for the agent.
  • meta-DO-NOT-FEED-TO-AGENT.txt: held back on purpose. It's used to test provenance tracking.

docs.title: 2. Watch the current-state wiki build
docs.text:
While the agent reads, open Current Process in the left navigation and follow the pages as it writes them: Overview, Business Rules, Compliance, Data Inputs Outputs, Exception Handling, Metrics, Pain Points, Scheduling and Triggers and Source Inventory.

The files appear one by one. When it's done, the agent tells you the source-grounded facts are written and it's synchronizing the task list.

docs.title: 3. Check the provenance on a captured item
docs.text:
Open Pain Points and expand Sources and Metadata at the top of the page.

You can see which agent captured each item and when, the source documents and the exact sections it came from, and the file metadata. This provenance stays attached for the whole life of the Map of Work.

docs.title: 4. Choose the map format, then read the task list
docs.text:
1. The agent asks how today's process should be mapped. It offers a case map (recommended), a BPMN model or a simple flow. Read its reasoning, then pick case map.

  2. Open the Task list panel. You'll see a readiness count, plus how many rows are confirmed, pending, sourced from documents, need confirmation or are missing. Yellow tags mark anything the agent assumed from process knowledge rather than took from your documents.

Next: Design the future state

docs.title: 1. Steer the level of detail on one task
docs.text:
In the AS-IS design, find the task Reapprove Claim Scope. It's too shallow, so ask for more detail:

On task "Reapprove Claim Scope" please expand that task into its logical steps, at least 3 no more than 5, for greater granularity.

The task becomes a four-step sequence: report scope mismatch, review changed scope, reapprove it and return to repair. The diagram is redrawn around it.

docs.title: 2. Confirm the AS-IS
docs.text:
Cartographer needs an explicit confirmation of the current state before it moves on to the future state. Send:

I confirm the AS-IS process.

docs.title: 3. Ask for the future state
docs.text:
Once you've confirmed the AS-IS, send:

Lets proceed with the to-be future state design. Call out all your proposed changes, transformations along with the reasons why they are being proposed especially as relates to kpis, objectives, pain points or business goals.

The agent consults process knowledge and finds an eleven-stage reference baseline to design against. It confirms a case is still the best execution style. Then it makes its first value argument: for P1 outages, run containment, entitlement, evidence and parts in parallel, instead of waiting behind a weekly coverage date. That's in service of the 24-hour P1 objective.

If it asks which future-state design to build, pick Case management (Recommended).

If the agent doesn't recommend parallel work for P1 outages, question it:

So what is your improvement idea for  P1 OUTAGES?

Then propose it yourself:

Would it make sense to run containment, entitlement, evidence and parts in parallel, instead of waiting behind a weekly coverage date? Or is that what you already proposed?

Finally, ask it to update the design:

Update the future-state design to show explicit parallel P1 workstreams

This one takes a while

The future-state pass runs for several minutes. A good moment for a coffee.

docs.title: 4. Review the Transformation Decisions
docs.text:
Open Transformation Decisions under Future Design and walk through three or four rows.

Each change gets its own row: the AS-IS area, the AS-IS issue, the proposed target change, and a User decision column that stays at Proposed — Future Process Review until you confirm it. Every change is argued against a specific number: 24-hour P1 downtime, 2.3 days of intake and asset uncertainty, a 4.2-day coverage decision, first-time fix and auditability, or the 22% of repeat failures that never reach quality investigation.

Why this matters

This table shows whether the tool ties each change to business value or only redraws the diagram.

docs.title: 5. Review the open questions
docs.text:
Open Resources > Knowledge > Queries > Open Questions in the left navigation.

This page collects everything Cartographer couldn't confirm from your evidence: checks on the current process, safe assumptions to confirm, and open decisions for the TO-BE, such as Finance's tolerance for cost variance. Each item is a question for a person, so the list tells you who you still need to talk to before the design is signed off.

Next: Make live edits and verify them

docs.title: Generate the PDD and trace it
1. Generate and download the PDD
docs.text:
1. Ask for the process document. Wait for it to generate and for the independent review to finish.

  2. Download it as Word and open it.

The document opens with the problem statement and the objectives the project was given. You'll spot two objectives that were added mid-session: the 20% variance rule was taken up as an objective in its own right. Then come the expected value, acceptance targets, scope boundaries, the current flow with its metrics, and the impact of each pain point.

docs.title: 2. Trace your own edits in the PDD
docs.text:
1. Scroll to the target flow and the What Changes AS-IS to TO-BE table.

    Every task in every stage has a type. That's the to-do list for the SDD. The What Changes table ties each change to the goal it serves and the metric it moves.

  2. Keep scrolling. You'll find the business rules (including the one you added live), the data model entities, a data dictionary lifted from the claim form, integrations, RACI, exceptions, human-in-the-loop and Action Center tasks, the compliance and regulatory matrix, and the KPI acceptance criteria.

  3. Find both of your edits: the 20% variance rule, and the task you expanded earlier.

Why this matters

The PDD carries everything an SDD needs, each item traced back to the evidence and to the KPI it moves. That's what you'll build the SDD from next.

Next: Generate the SDD

docs.title: 1. Ask for the SDD
docs.text:
Once the PDD looks good, generate the Solution Design Document (SDD):

Generate the SDD.

The first clarifying question asks how you want the generation itself to run, meaning how often it should pause for you along the way:

  • Autonomous generates the full SDD and only interrupts for hard blockers.
  • Interactive pauses at the summary, architecture and final SDD checkpoints instead.

Either is a valid choice. Interactive gives you more control points, and Autonomous trades them for speed.

docs.title: 2. Bring in Maestro Flow while it runs
docs.text:
While the SDD is being generated, send this prompt and click Steer to push it in early:

I would also like to orchestrate one of the stages using Maestro Flow. Which one would be better fitted?

Cartographer recommends the stages that fit Maestro Flow best and explains why. Choose the ones you prefer. For example:

Update the SDD to USE Maestro Flow for both "Asset, Entitlement and Evidence Readiness" AND the cost-reconciliation

docs.title: 3. Refine the SDD, or bring your own template
docs.text:
The SDD isn't final until it works for you. Read it, and ask for changes the same way you shaped the TO-BE. You can even hand Cartographer your own SDD template and ask it to follow that structure.

  1. Download the example template, or use your own team's template:

    Download the SDD template (.docx)

  2. Attach the template and send:

    Can we modify the SDD cause it's not very easy to read. Would you be able to follow the attached template?

  3. Be specific about what's missing. For example:

    The current SDD doesn't contain the diagram nor process overview, activities, artefacts (suggested projects, possible assets and storage buckets), integrated components, error handling, triggers, project structure, testing strategy and next steps. I would expect to see the 2 Flow processes detailed here too

docs.title: 4. Publish the PDD and SDD
docs.text:
1. Choose to publish both documents to Automation Hub if you're prompted. If you aren't, ask Cartographer to do it, for example:

    upload the PDD and SDD to Automation Hub

  2. Cartographer verifies the upload and gives you links to the new entry in Automation Hub. The confirmation lists the process ID and the document IDs for the PDD and the SDD, and offers two follow-ups: Show me the published Automation Hub record and Download the published PDD and SDD.

Next: Ask a teammate (optional)

docs.title: How Cartographer works
docs.text:
Map the work once. Generate everything from it. With UiPath Cartographer, business analysts become cartographers. Instead of weeks of interviews and a blank canvas, a guided, AI-powered discovery conversation turns scattered process knowledge into one living definition of how the work runs: the Map of Work.

Bring what you have

  • SOPs and policies
  • Recorded walkthroughs
  • Workshop notes
  • Task captures

Cartographer

  • Starts with context: universal, domain and your own knowledge
  • Asks only what's missing
  • Reconciles your evidence and flags contradictions
  • Brings in the experts who know the answer

Map of Work

People, stages, systems and data, rules, exceptions, judgment and goals. Versioned, with a named owner and approver, and provenance on every fact.

Generated from the map

  • PDD for decision-makers
  • SDD for developers and coding agents
  • Best-fit canvas: Case, BPMN or Flow, with the reasoning behind it

Three ideas make the result something you can trust and build from:

  • Every fact is attributable. Each element carries its source and the person who verified it. Contradictions get resolved, not averaged.
  • No blank page. Cartographer already knows the usual shape of a process in your industry, and Process Atlas brings expert-attested maps you adapt rather than draw. It only asks what it can't work out.
  • Change the map, regenerate. Your documents are generated from the Map of Work, so nothing downstream drifts out of sync with how the business actually runs.

You'll see every one of these in action in this exercise.

Next: About Cobalt Ridge Automation

docs.title: Make live edits and verify them
1. Make the agentic edit, and use Steer
docs.text:
1. In the future-state design (TO-BE), find the finance human task Post and reconcile cost. Send:

    "Post and reconcile cost" is listed as a human task. Change this to be conducted by an agent with human verification when variance exceeds 25% of total cost.

  2. Before the agent finishes thinking, change the threshold. Send:

    actually when variance exceeds 20%

    The agent is probably halfway through a multi-step validation pass. There's no point waiting for a pass that's about to be outdated, so click Steer on the queued message to push your request in early.

  3. The request is accepted as a refinement. The agent updates the future case design, the business rules, the agentic task list and the transformation list. Then a second agent runs an independent review of the first one's work.

Compliance guardrails

Every request is checked against known compliance rules, from regulators or from the company. If a change broke one, for example no agent may approve any variance, Cartographer would refuse it and explain why.

docs.title: 2. Verify the change landed everywhere
docs.text:
Run three checks:

  1. The TO-BE diagram. Find the Cost closure and quality stage. Post and reconcile cost now carries an AI agent tag, followed by Verify Variance as a human action for variances over 20%. Check that nothing else in the process moved.

  2. Business Rules in the wiki. The new business rule is there, and it's confirmed.

  3. Transformation Decisions. Your change is correctly absent. It was your explicit instruction, not a transformation the agent proposed.

Next: Generate and trace the PDD

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin

Have these ready before the session:

  • A machine with Cartographer: the workshop VM, or your own machine with Cartographer installed.
  • Your UiPath account: you'll use it to sign in to the UiPath Assistant.
  • Access to the workshop environment: in this workshop we use https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs/CartographerWorkshop. Talk to your trainer if you haven't received an invitation.

docs.title: 1. Using a VM
docs.text:
If you don't have Cartographer installed on your own machine, connect to the virtual machine your trainer provides. Prior to the training, you'll receive an email with an invitation to a UiPath Studio & Robot sandbox environment.

After you confirm your attendance, the sandbox gets created and you can open it.

docs.title: Optional: you might need to Register your VM
docs.text:
1. In the Windows search bar, type Email & accounts.
  2. Click Add a work or school account.
  3. Sign in with your UiPath account.

docs.title: 2. Using your own machine
docs.text:
If you prefer to use your own machine, make sure it meets these prerequisites:

  • Windows, with UiPath Assistant STS version 26.10.202 or later, installed from the "Studio, Assistant and Robot STS" download in Automation Cloud. The Cartographer tab doesn't appear in LTS versions (2025.10 or older).
  • Assistant installed with the Robot in attended (user) mode. Sign-in doesn't work when the Robot runs as a Windows service.
  • PowerShell allowed on the machine, since Cartographer uses it to start.
  • A UiPath user license other than Express.

docs.title: 3. Open the Assistant
docs.text:
1. Open the UiPath Assistant and sign in with your UiPath account (via Microsoft).
  2. Connect to the CartographerWorkshop tenant at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs.

Working self-paced?

You can connect to any other environment and tenant you have access to.

Next: Set up the project

docs.title: Set up the project and check its knowledge
1. Create the project and give it the brief
docs.text:
1. Open Cartographer. On the home screen, click the + icon next to Business Processes in the left panel.

  2. The New project dialog opens. It has a Name field and a Project instructions box that already contains a generic default paragraph.

  3. In Name, type:

    Cobalt Warranty Resolution from Outage Intake to Restored Outcome

  4. In Project instructions, leave the default paragraph where it is. Paste the brief below straight after it, so the box reads as one continuous set of instructions:

    #context:
Cobalt Ridge Automation handles approximately 7,400 warranty claims each year across industrial automation and material-handling equipment. The current process takes a mean 11.4 days from customer report to restored line, with mean P1 downtime of 96 hours, while data and work are fragmented across Cobalt Ridge Support Cloud (CRSC), WarrantyTrack WT-9, AssetVault, Helios CRM, SAP S/4HANA, FieldLink FSM, and email. Manual re-keying, a weekly coverage gate, undocumented parts substitutions, late cost posting, and weak repeat-failure linkage drive rework, customer-credit exposure, and $23.8M of annual warranty spend.

# Objectives

- Reduce mean resolution time from 11.4 days to 3.5 days by FY2027 through an immediate coordination case, six sequential primary stages, conditional supporting stages, automated follow-up, and visible handoffs.

- Reduce P1 line downtime from 96 hours to 24 hours by FY2027 through impact triage, managed containment, field-work coordination, and restoration validation.

- Replace email-only work handoffs with a coordination case linked to WT-9, while retaining human authority for coverage, safety, engineering, substitution, restoration, and finance decisions.

- Improve evidence completeness, decision traceability, cost-reconciliation visibility, and repeat-failure learning through active stages, timing controls, and linked quality work.

  5. Check that the dialog now shows your title and the full instructions.

  6. Leave Context files empty and Approval mode at its default, then click Create.

You now have an empty Business Analysis project with no conversations yet. Your instructions sit in the Project instructions panel on the right.

docs.title: 2. Ask what it already knows, before uploading anything
docs.text:
Don't upload anything yet. Paste this into the composer and send it:

Verify your process-knowledge / process-skills and answer only from it:

(1) the 3 KPIs that typically matter most for industrial-equipment warranty resolution, with reference baselines and targets;

(2) the compliance and audit controls this process must enforce;

(3) the persona titles who run it, by stage;

(4) where UiPath best-practice suggests Document Understanding vs. DMN / business rules vs. AI Agent.

The agent consults its Process Knowledge and answers all four parts. You get KPIs with reference baselines plus good and stretch targets, a list of controls, personas by stage, and a component-placement table covering Document Understanding, DMN and business rules, AI agents and human-in-the-loop.

Why this matters

Anything that comes from process knowledge rather than from your own documents is flagged as not confirmed. Cartographer never passes off a general industry assumption as one of your facts.

Next: Capture and review the AS-IS
